Stage 3 · Reading

The net that drinks fog

An award-winning design on a Moroccan mountain — and why the clever part is not the technology.

🌌💧
1 · Before you read. A village in a dry region gets running water for the first time. Which change would you expect to matter most?

Choose one and say why. Compare with a partner before you read.Choose one and say why before you read.Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

The net that drinks fog

Written for this course, from the Wasserstiftung (German Water Foundation) project reports on Mount Boutmezguida, the UNFCCC Momentum for Change citation (2016), and Dar Si Hmad’s own project documentation.

1On Mount Boutmezguida, in the Anti-Atlas range of southwest Morocco, thick fog is pushed inland from the Atlantic on most mornings for about six months of the year. The mountain stands at 1,225 metres and receives well under 150 millimetres of rain in an average year. The phenomenon had been described for decades and was used by nobody. Today the moisture is caught in nets on the ridge, and the water is piped more than twenty kilometres down to villages where, until 2015, every litre had been carried up by hand or bought from a tanker.

2The design is almost embarrassingly simple. Panels of mesh are attached to steel frames along the ridge; fog is driven through them by the wind; droplets condense on the threads, run down into a gutter and are stored in cisterns below. Nothing is burnt. No electricity is generated or consumed by the collection itself. On a foggy day the installation now yields around 37,000 litres, and the whole system was built without a single moving part.

3Getting it to survive was the hard bit. Earlier fog nets in the region were repeatedly destroyed by the wind, and the more efficient the mesh was made, the more damaging that wind became. The version now in use, developed over more than two years by a German industrial designer working for a water foundation in Munich, is held by tensioners and shock cords and is rated to withstand gusts of 120 kilometres an hour. It was also designed to be repaired by the people who use it. Residents are trained on site, and the installation is run by the community rather than by a contractor. That is the inventive part, and it is the part visitors miss.

4The effect on the villages has been remarkable, and it is not mainly an effect on health. In a region where drought is normal, whether the fog arrives affects the shape of the whole day. Water had been fetched from distant wells by women and girls, who lost up to four hours of every day to the walk. Those hours were returned overnight. Girls who had been kept out of school by the journey were sent back to it; the time released was spent on argan oil and on paid work. When the project was recognised by the United Nations in 2016, it was honoured under a category for women’s-leadership results rather than for engineering.

5The scale is modest and is usually overstated by people who write about it. Fewer than a hundred and fifty households were connected in the first phase. Fog harvesting works only where fog, altitude, terrain and community support happen to line up, and it is not offered by its own engineers as a general answer to water scarcity. What is striking is how much was achieved by a technology that could have been built in 1950.

6Perhaps that is the point. An invention is usually called innovative when it is complicated, and this one was praised for inventiveness of exactly the opposite kind: a functional object with no pump, no fuel and nothing to break, kept working by the households it supplies. The technology is impressive but old. What was actually designed here was the arrangement around it.

Text A · How the water is caught

Written for this course, from the Wasserstiftung project reports on Mount Boutmezguida and Dar Si Hmad’s project documentation.

On Mount Boutmezguida, in the Anti-Atlas range of southwest Morocco, thick fog is pushed inland from the Atlantic on most mornings for about six months of the year. The mountain stands at 1,225 metres and receives well under 150 millimetres of rain in an average year. The phenomenon had been described for decades and was used by nobody. Today the moisture is caught in nets on the ridge, and the water is piped more than twenty kilometres down to villages where, until 2015, every litre had been carried up by hand or bought from a tanker.

The design is almost embarrassingly simple. Panels of mesh are attached to steel frames along the ridge; fog is driven through them by the wind; droplets condense on the threads, run down into a gutter and are stored in cisterns below. Nothing is burnt. No electricity is generated or consumed by the collection itself. On a foggy day the installation now yields around 37,000 litres, and the whole system was built without a single moving part.

Getting it to survive was the hard bit. Earlier fog nets in the region were repeatedly destroyed by the wind, and the more efficient the mesh was made, the more damaging that wind became. The version now in use, developed over more than two years by a German industrial designer working for a water foundation in Munich, is held by tensioners and shock cords and is rated to withstand gusts of 120 kilometres an hour. It was also designed to be repaired by the people who use it: residents are trained on site, and the installation is run by the community rather than by a contractor.

Text B · What the water changed

Written for this course, from the UNFCCC Momentum for Change citation (2016) and Dar Si Hmad’s project documentation.

The effect on the villages has been remarkable, and it is not mainly an effect on health. In a region where drought is normal, whether the fog arrives affects the shape of the whole day. Water had been fetched from distant wells by women and girls, who lost up to four hours of every day to the walk. Those hours were returned overnight. Girls who had been kept out of school by the journey were sent back to it; the time released was spent on argan oil and on paid work. When the project was recognised by the United Nations in 2016, it was honoured under a category for women’s-leadership results rather than for engineering.

The scale is modest and is usually overstated by people who write about it. Fewer than a hundred and fifty households were connected in the first phase. Fog harvesting works only where fog, altitude, terrain and community support happen to line up, and it is not offered by its own engineers as a general answer to water scarcity. What is striking is how much was achieved by a technology that could have been built in 1950.

Perhaps that is the point. An invention is usually called innovative when it is complicated, and this one was praised for inventiveness of exactly the opposite kind: a functional object with no pump, no fuel and nothing to break, kept working by the households it supplies. The technology is impressive but old. What was actually designed here was the arrangement around it — the training, the ownership and the repairs — and that is the part which is hardest to copy somewhere else.

Every passive is the same two parts: a form of be, and a past participle. Everything else is choosing which noun goes first.

1 · Read the explanation.
How the passive is built, and why it is chosen

A passive is always the same two parts: a form of be, and the past participle of the main verb. The tense is carried entirely by be, so once you can conjugate be, you can build every passive in the language: is collected, was collected, is being collected, has been collected, had been collected, will be collected, can be collected, to be collected.

What happens to the sentence. The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive one: Storms tore the nets apart → The nets were torn apart by storms. The original subject either disappears or moves to the end after by. Only verbs that take an object can do this, which is why arrive, happen, fall and exist have no passive at all.

Why writers choose it. Three reasons, none of them about formality. The doer may be unknown (the frames were damaged in the night); the doer may be obvious or irrelevant (the water is piped down to the village — nobody is interested in the plumber); or the thing may simply be what the paragraph is about, and English likes the topic at the front (the mesh was then made stronger). Add by + agent only when the agent is news.

Two objects. Verbs such as give, award, offer, send, show and tell have two objects, so two passives are possible: The project was awarded a prize and A prize was awarded to the project. The first is far commoner, because the person or thing receiving is usually the topic.

Get instead of be. In speech, get replaces be for sudden or unwelcome events: the panel got damaged, she got promoted. It is informal, and it is not used in reports.

The commonest errors at this level
  • Leaving out be: The nets torn apart by storms — there is no passive without it.
  • Past simple instead of participle: was tore, was broke, have been wrote.
  • Making an intransitive verb passive: The accident was happened.
  • Adding by when nobody needs it: The water is collected by people.
  • Losing the tense: has been installed is not the same as was installed.

Two things to watch

1 — The participle, not the past. Was tore, was broke, have been wrote are the three commonest passive errors in the world, and all three are the same mistake: the second form of the verb where the third is needed. Torn, broken, written.

2 — Do not use it to hide. Mistakes were made is grammatical and empty. In your own writing, ask whether the agent is missing because it is irrelevant or because you would rather not say. The first is style; the second is something the reader usually notices.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Turning an active sentence into a passive one

Active: Storms had torn the early nets apart before the second winter.

Step 1 — find the object. Ask what the storms tore apart: the early nets. That noun becomes the subject of the new sentence.

Step 2 — keep the tense. The active is past perfect (had torn), so be goes into the past perfect: had been.

Step 3 — add the participle. Tear → tore → torn. Never the middle form.

Step 4 — decide about the agent. Here the storms are the whole point, so keep them: by storms. If the doer were somebody, people or they, you would drop it.

Passive: The early nets had been torn apart by storms before the second winter.

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
One rule, every tense

Every passive is a form of be + a past participle. The tense lives in be and nothing else changes: is collected, is being tested, was torn, were being built, has been installed, had been supplied, will be replaced, is going to be raised, can be repaired, should have been tested, to be tested. If you can form be in a tense, you can form the passive in it.

Only verbs with an object can go passive. They collect the water → The water is collected; but arrive, happen, occur, appear, rise, fall take no object, so An accident was happened is impossible. With two objects you have a choice of subject: They awarded the project a prize → The project was awarded a prize or A prize was awarded to the project.

Why a writer chooses it

The passive is not a politer active. It changes what the sentence is about, by putting the affected thing in the subject position where the reader looks first. Writers use it when the doer is unknown (The nets were torn apart), obvious (Forty panels have been installed — by installers, plainly), irrelevant in a description of a process, or when they want to keep the topic steady across sentences: The mesh collects the water. It is then channelled into tanks and filtered before use.

by + agent appears only when the doer is news: The nets were torn apart by storms. Adding it out of habit weakens the sentence, which is why The water is collected by people reads badly. In lab reports and instructions the passive is the default register; in a complaint or a news lead it can be a way of hiding responsibility, and a careful reader notices.

Errors to watch: The panels have installed → have been installed · It was happened last year → It happened · The mesh is been tested → is being tested · It should be tested by somebody last week → should have been tested.

1 · Read the model entry.
Model · an entry for a design award

The object is a clay pot inside a second clay pot, with wet sand between them. Vegetables are kept in the inner pot, the sand is dampened twice a day, and a wet cloth is laid over the top. As the moisture evaporates from the sand, heat is drawn out of the inner pot, and the temperature inside is held about fourteen degrees below the temperature of the room. Nothing is burnt, and no electricity is generated or consumed.

The problem it solves is not storage but income. In markets where there is no refrigeration, tomatoes have to be sold on the day they are picked, and the price is set by whoever is buying. With the pots, the same tomatoes can be held for three weeks, and the seller decides when to sell.

The first version was fired at too low a temperature and cracked in the sun, so the clay was changed and the walls were made thicker. A lid was added after the second season, when it was found that most of the water was being lost from the top.

What is most striking is what has been left out. There is no pump, no filter and no part that has to be replaced. It should win because it can be made, mended and understood entirely in the place where it is used.
